slide.title: Drop a pin on North Korea

slide.heading: The next map mixes three years as colors: red = 2013, green = 2003, blue = 1993. A place lit in all three years looks...

slides.notes: Answer: B, white. Red, green and blue at full brightness add up to white, so stable old lights are white. The next quiz asks about new lights.
slides.title: The next map mixes three years as colors: red = 2013, green = 2003, blue = 1993. A place lit in all three years looks...

slide.heading: Same map. A place dark in 1993 and 2003 but lit in 2013 looks...

slides.notes: Answer: C, red, because red is 2013 only. Yellow (red plus green) means lit since 2003. On the next slide, much of China is red and yellow, Japan is white, and North Korea stays dark.
slides.title: Same map. A place dark in 1993 and 2003 but lit in 2013 looks...
Why are the lights different? (RGB composite, 1993 to 2013)

slide.heading: RGB app stop: name a city or region that lit up recently (red or yellow) and its country.

slides.notes: The second hands-on stop, about six minutes. Students open https://jhowarth.users.earthengine.app/view/rgb-nighttime-lights and look for red or yellow places. Good finds: inland China, parts of India, the Gulf, West Africa. Ask what changed there between 1993 and 2013.
slides.title: RGB app stop: name a city or region that lit up recently (red or yellow) and its country.
Better Night Lights Data, For Longer (John Gibson)
slides.notes: Play 2 minutes.

slide.heading: Which sensor gives sharper night lights, with less blurring and no top-coding in city centers?

slides.notes: Answer: B, VIIRS. DMSP blurs light into nearby areas and caps bright city centers, so it understates inequality and growth in dense places. Gibson argues for VIIRS, and for VIIRS-like series that extend it back in time. Landsat is a daytime sensor.
slides.title: Which sensor gives sharper night lights, with less blurring and no top-coding in city centers?

Shining a light on economic inequality (University of Waikato)

slide.title: Night lights work equally well in dense cities and in sparsely populated rural areas.

config.question: Night lights work equally well in dense cities and in sparsely populated rural areas.

slides.notes: Answer: False. In sparse rural areas, much economic activity (farming) emits little light, so lights understate rural output. The Waikato video makes this point with the United States.
slides.title: Night lights work equally well in dense cities and in sparsely populated rural areas.

We can also use daytime images: why and how?

slide.title: What can daytime images show that night lights cannot?

slides.notes: Two minutes of ideas, then voting. Expected: roof materials, building size, roads, crops, water and green space, all visible in rural areas where night lights are dark. Machine learning turns these features into poverty estimates (next slides).
slides.title: What can daytime images show that night lights cannot?
Monitoring regional development from outer space

slide.heading: Which images fit each task best?

slides.notes: Answer: nighttime images for city brightness and electrification; daytime images for roofs and crops. The slide summary pairs nighttime images with urban development and daytime images with rural development.
slides.title: Which images fit each task best?
slides.answer: Nighttime images: Brightness of a growing city, Electrification of towns; Daytime images: Roof materials in a village, Crop fields and farmland
